analysis.one_liner: Taxed half of oil companies' hurricane-driven windfall profits to fund Katrina and Rita relief.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in October 2005, never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died when the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: After Hurricanes Katrina and Rita, oil prices spiked and major oil companies posted record profits. Senator Chuck Schumer proposed a temporary tax on half of those windfall profits — the amount above what the companies earned on average from 2000 to 2004 — with the money dedicated to paying for hurricane relief spending. The bill applied only to 2005 and 2006, hit big integrated oil companies and any crude-oil producer or refiner with over $100 million in sales, and the revenue would flow into a dedicated Hurricane Relief Trust Fund. It never got a hearing in the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Hurricane Katrina and Rita victims and federal taxpayers. The tax would have raised revenue from oil companies' sudden profits and used it to offset the cost of hurricane relief, reducing the burden on the general treasury. Anyone who pays federal taxes or depended on relief spending gains if the bill passes.

how_it_helps.text: It imposed a 50% excise tax on oil companies' windfall profit — taxable income above their inflated 2000-2004 average profit plus 10% — for 2005 and 2006 only [S2] [S3].

The revenue would go into a Hurricane Relief Trust Fund, available without further appropriation to offset supplemental spending bills for Katrina and Rita victims enacted before January 1, 2008 [S3].

It applied to integrated oil companies and any producer or refiner of crude oil with over $100 million in gross receipts, capturing the major companies whose profits spiked after the hurricanes, and treated commonly controlled businesses as one company to prevent evasion through affiliates [S3].
Leftover funds not spent by the end of 2008 would be credited back to the general fund as regular tax receipts, so the money could not sit unused [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Integrated oil companies and large crude-oil producers and refiners, which would have paid a 50% tax on profits above their recent-average baseline for 2005 and 2006. Any cost passed through to consumers at the pump would land on drivers, though the tax was temporary and limited to above-normal profits.

drawbacks.text: Windfall profits taxes are notoriously hard to define: the bill taxed income above an average-plus-10% baseline, and companies could shift income, timing, and accounting across years and affiliates, inviting disputes and games [S3].

Oil companies could pass some of the tax through to consumers in higher prices, and the tax could discourage domestic production or refining investment during an energy squeeze — a lesson often drawn from the 1980 windfall profits tax experience.
The bill allowed companies to deduct the windfall tax as a business expense, softening its bite and complicating its revenue math [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a temporary, targeted response: it would have clawed back a portion of profits that spiked because of a national disaster and steered that money to relief spending, at a modest risk of slightly higher fuel prices and administrative complexity. The tax was limited to two years and to profits above a normal baseline, so it avoided a permanent new tax burden. The main honest objection is design risk — windfall taxes invite gaming and possible pass-through to consumers — but the potential cost to ordinary people was small compared with the relief funding it would have supplied.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Senator Schumer introduced the bill on October 3, 2005, in the weeks after Hurricanes Katrina and Rita drove oil prices to record highs [S1] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill died in committee without a hearing or vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil companies, which kept the full amount of their post-hurricane windfall profits untaxed. The Treasury and hurricane relief spending were funded by general taxpayers instead of by the industry's excess earnings.

against.name: Major integrated oil companies
against.role: Integrated crude oil producers and refiners
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed windfall profits tax proposals after the 2005 hurricanes and lobbied against them

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no party bloc ever took a position on the floor.

industries.note: The bill would have taxed 50% of their profits above a 2000-2004 baseline for 2005 and 2006, directly reducing the record earnings they posted after the hurricanes raised prices. Their gain from the bill dying was ordinary taxpayers footing the relief bill instead.

Any producer or refiner of crude oil with over $100 million in gross receipts would have owed the windfall tax, though common-control rules treated affiliated businesses as one company. This narrower segment would have faced the same two-year tax on above-baseline profits.
